meta.title: way1ong Sky — a flight through the Solar System
meta.description: Fly between the Sun, the planets and the Moon — where they really are today. Free, no ads, no tracking.

app.name: Sky
app.scene: The Solar System in 3D. Drag to look around, pinch or scroll to come closer; pick a body from the list to fly to it.

scale.label: Scale
scale.handyNote: Handy scale: distances squeezed, bodies enlarged — everything fits one look. Directions are real.
scale.trueNote: True scale: sizes and distances as they are. The planets are specks in an emptiness — fly to one to see it.

time.label: Time
time.noSpin: At this speed the bodies’ spin about their own axes is not shown: it would only flicker. Their motion along the orbits is real.
time.limit: The app’s calendar ends here: it runs from {from} to {to}.

lunarAt.total: {date}: a total lunar eclipse. The whole Moon is in the Earth’s shadow. Time is stopped — let it run to watch the shadow leave.
lunarAt.partial: {date}: a partial lunar eclipse. Part of the Moon is in the Earth’s shadow. Time is stopped — let it run to watch the shadow move.

solarAt.total: {date}: a total solar eclipse. The dark spot on the Earth is the Moon’s shadow. Time is stopped — let it run to watch the spot cross the Earth.
solarAt.annular: {date}: an annular solar eclipse. The dim spot on the Earth is the Moon’s shadow; a ring of the Sun stays visible there. Time is stopped — let it run to watch the spot cross the Earth.
solarAt.partial: {date}: a partial solar eclipse. The dim patch on the Earth is the edge of the Moon’s shadow. Time is stopped — let it run to watch it move.

about.sun: The Sun is the star at the heart of our solar system, and the only star in it. It is a huge ball of hydrogen and helium held together by its own gravity, and it holds 99.8% of the solar system’s mass. Its gravity keeps everything in orbit, from the biggest planets to the smallest bits of debris.
about.mercury: Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun and the smallest one, only slightly larger than the Earth’s Moon. Days there reach 430 °C; with no atmosphere to keep the heat, nights drop to −180 °C. It is the fastest planet: it goes around the Sun in 88 Earth days.
about.venus: Venus is the second planet from the Sun and the Earth’s closest planetary neighbor; in our sky it is the third brightest object after the Sun and the Moon. It is similar to the Earth in structure and size, but its thick atmosphere traps heat and makes it the hottest planet, with a surface hot enough to melt lead. Venus spins slowly, and in the opposite direction from most planets.
about.earth: The Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the biggest of the four planets closest to it, all made of rock and metal. It is the only place we know of inhabited by living things, and the only planet in the solar system with liquid water on its surface. Its atmosphere is 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 1% other gases, and it shields us from much of the Sun’s harmful radiation.
about.moon: The Moon is the Earth’s only natural satellite. It spins at the same rate as it goes around the Earth, so the same side always faces us; people first saw the far side in 1959, when a Soviet spacecraft flew past. Its surface is solid and rocky, cratered and pitted by impacts of asteroids, meteorites and comets.
about.mars: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun. It is called the Red Planet: iron minerals in its dirt oxidize, or rust, and make the surface look red. It is one of the most explored bodies in the solar system and the only planet where rovers have been sent; NASA missions have found lots of evidence that billions of years ago Mars was much wetter and warmer, with a thicker atmosphere.
about.jupiter: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the largest in the solar system — more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined. Its stripes and swirls are cold, windy clouds of ammonia and water in an atmosphere of hydrogen and helium. The Great Red Spot is a giant storm bigger than the Earth that has raged for hundreds of years.
about.saturn: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun and the second largest. Like Jupiter, it is a massive ball made mostly of hydrogen and helium. It is not the only planet with rings, but none are as spectacular or as complex as Saturn’s. It is the farthest planet from the Earth discovered by the unaided eye, known since ancient times.
about.uranus: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun and the third largest — a very cold and windy world. It rotates at a nearly 90-degree angle from the plane of its orbit, so it appears to spin sideways, rolling around the Sun like a ball. It was the first planet found with the aid of a telescope: the astronomer William Herschel discovered it in 1781.
about.neptune: Neptune is the eighth and most distant planet from the Sun, more than 30 times as far from it as the Earth. It is a dark, cold ice giant whipped by supersonic winds, and the only planet in our solar system not visible to the naked eye. It was discovered in 1846 and completed its first orbit around the Sun since then in 2011.

text.sun: In Latin the Sun is “sol”, and the Sun god of the ancient Greeks was Helios: words like “solar” and “heliosphere” come from them. Several spacecraft watch the Sun; the SOHO observatory has done so since its launch in 1995. In 2021 NASA’s Parker Solar Probe became the first spacecraft to fly through the corona, the Sun’s upper atmosphere.
text.mercury: Mercury is named for the swiftest of the ancient Roman gods; it is one of the five bright planets the Romans could see in the sky. The first spacecraft to visit it was NASA’s Mariner 10, launched in 1973; the first to orbit it was MESSENGER, launched in 2004. In 2018 Europe and Japan launched BepiColombo, a joint mission of two spacecraft.
text.venus: Venus is named for the ancient Roman goddess of love and beauty — the only planet named after a female god. The ancients took it for two objects, a morning star and an evening star. Its phases, first observed by Galileo through his telescope, gave the key proof that the planets go round the Sun. On December 14, 1962, NASA’s Mariner 2 flew past Venus — the first visit of a spacecraft to another planet. Between 1961 and 1984 ten Soviet Venera probes reached its surface.
text.earth: Earth is the only planet whose English name does not come from Greek or Roman mythology: the word is about 1,000 years old and simply means “the ground”. Every language has its own name for our planet. Today many spacecraft in orbit study the Earth as a whole system — the atmosphere, the ocean, the glaciers and the solid ground.
text.moon: The Moon shares its name with all moons because people did not know of others until Galileo discovered four moons of Jupiter in 1610. In 1959 the Soviet Luna 1 was the first spacecraft to fly by the Moon, in 1966 Luna 9 made the first soft landing, and in 1969 Apollo 11 landed the first people. From 1969 to 1972 twelve American astronauts walked on the Moon. In April 2026 Artemis II carried four astronauts around its far side.
text.mars: The ancient Romans named Mars for their god of war because its reddish color reminded them of blood; the Egyptians called it “Her Desher”, the red one. In the list of missions to Mars that NASA keeps, the first flyby that did not fail is Mariner 4, launched in 1964; the first orbiters were launched in 1971, and the first lander with a rover, Mars Pathfinder, in 1996. Mars is the only planet where rovers roam.
text.jupiter: Jupiter shines bright, so people have known it since ancient times; it is named for the king of the Roman gods. In 1610 Galileo Galilei made the first detailed observations of it with a small homemade telescope and saw its four largest moons. NASA’s first spacecraft to the outer planets, Pioneer 10, came closest to Jupiter on December 4, 1973. The Galileo spacecraft orbited the planet for almost eight years, and on July 4, 2016, Juno entered orbit around it.
text.saturn: Saturn is the farthest planet found by the unaided eye, known since ancient times; the oldest written records of it, about 700 BCE, are attributed to the Assyrians. It is named for the Roman god of agriculture. In 1610 Galileo saw its rings but took them for a “triple planet”; in 1655 Christiaan Huygens discovered the rings and the largest moon, Titan. Pioneer 11 was the first spacecraft to reach Saturn, on September 1, 1979; on July 1, 2004, Cassini became the first to orbit it, and on January 14, 2005, the Huygens probe landed on Titan.
text.uranus: Uranus was the first planet found with a telescope: the British astronomer William Herschel discovered it on March 13, 1781, taking it at first for a comet or a star. He wanted to name it after King George III, but the name suggested by Johann Bode — that of the Greek god of the sky — was the one that stayed. Only one spacecraft has visited it: on January 24, 1986, Voyager 2 passed 81,500 kilometers from its cloud tops and discovered 10 new moons and two new rings.
text.neptune: Neptune was the first planet found by calculation: Uranus did not move as expected, and the French mathematician Urbain Le Verrier worked out where an unknown planet should be. In 1846 Johann Galle at the Berlin Observatory found it on his first night of searching. Galileo had seen Neptune in 1612 and 1613 but recorded it as a fixed star. The planet is named for the Roman god of the sea. Only one spacecraft has studied it up close: Voyager 2, in 1989.

about.io: Io is the most volcanically active world in the solar system, with hundreds of volcanoes; some throw lava fountains dozens of kilometers high. It is caught between Jupiter’s massive gravity and the precisely timed pulls of its neighbors Europa and Ganymede. The volcanoes cover its face with new deposits faster than large craters can mark it. Voyager 1 spotted the first signs of this volcanism in 1979; most of what we know about Io comes from the Galileo spacecraft.
about.europa: There is strong evidence that the icy moon Europa has a saltwater ocean — perhaps one of the best places to look for environments where life could exist beyond Earth. Europa is the fourth largest of Jupiter’s moons. Most of what we know about it comes from the Galileo mission; on October 14, 2024, NASA launched Europa Clipper, the first mission to study Europa in detail.
about.ganymede: Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system, bigger even than the planet Mercury. It is the only moon known to have its own magnetic field, which causes auroras around its poles. The dark areas of its surface are older and heavily cratered, the light ones younger. There is strong evidence of an underground saltwater ocean that may hold more water than all of Earth’s surface. The Juno spacecraft photographed it in detail in June 2021.
about.callisto: Callisto is the most heavily cratered object in the solar system. It is Jupiter’s second largest moon and the third largest in the solar system. Data from the Galileo spacecraft in the 1990s showed that it may hide a salty ocean beneath its surface. Callisto and Jupiter’s three other largest moons were discovered in 1610 by the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei.

about.title: About
about.text: The bodies stand where they really are today; the positions are computed on your device. Nothing is sent anywhere: no ads, no tracking, no account.
about.textures: Maps of the Sun, the planets and the Moon, and the starry background: Solar System Scope, CC BY 4.0. The background is decoration: its stars are not placed by a catalogue.
about.moonMaps: Maps of Jupiter’s four moons: Credit: U.S. Geological Survey, from images of the Voyager and Galileo spacecraft; public domain. The maps are in shades of grey and have no images near the poles. The moons turn one side to Jupiter — which side is shown only roughly; the moons’ shadows and eclipses are not drawn.
about.facts: Sizes of the bodies and of Saturn’s rings: NASA fact sheets.
about.shadows: The Earth’s shadow on the Moon and the Moon’s on the Earth are computed from the real positions. The copper glow of the eclipsed Moon is a picture, not a measurement.
about.aim: “Point the phone” on the sky map is a trial. The program reads the phone’s tilt and compass on the device only and sends them nowhere. A phone’s compass is rough, so the sky on the screen may be shifted against the real one; the picture does not lean with the phone.
about.photos: Photos in the cards: NASA and its partners, named under each photo; some are cropped. This program is made independently of NASA.
about.sky: The sky from a place: stars — Wikidata (CC0); which stars are joined into constellations — d3-celestial by Olaf Frohn (BSD-3-Clause), after the charts of the IAU and Sky & Telescope; cities — Wikidata. Stars are drawn by day too, and the bending of light by the air near the horizon is not drawn. “Dark enough”, “in view” and “too faint for the eye” are the program’s own measures, not definitions of astronomy. For some stars Wikidata has no visual brightness: there the close Gaia G brightness is used. Proper names of stars: the names approved by the International Astronomical Union, from the list in Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0), and the titles of the stars’ articles in Wikipedia.
about.stories: The stories of the constellations and the line on who listed each constellation are written after Wikipedia’s articles and table — the links stand under each card. The texts of the stories may be used under the same licence, CC BY-SA 4.0. The brightest star, the month of the best evenings and the height of a constellation are worked out by the program itself.
about.art: The drawings of the constellations are cards of the star atlas “Urania’s Mirror” (engraved by Sidney Hall, 1825) from Wikimedia Commons, public domain; the scans were restored by Adam Cuerden. From cards that show several constellations the figure needed is cut out. Under each drawing there is a link to the page of its file.
about.deep: Galaxies, nebulae and star clusters on the sky map: what they are, how far and how bright — after NASA’s pages of Hubble’s Messier Catalog; where they are — Wikidata (CC0); the photographs — NASA, ESA and the Space Telescope Science Institute, each named under its photograph.
about.instruments: The section “Instruments of astronomers”: the texts are our own, written after Wikipedia’s articles in three languages and the pages of NASA and ESA; under each card are the links to its sources. The drawings are made for the program and are not to scale. The texts of the cards written after Wikipedia may be used on the terms of
about.far: Beyond the Solar System: the Milky Way from outside is an artist’s concept (NASA/JPL-Caltech), not a photograph; the Sun’s place and the scale are taken from the grid of the same picture. The clusters, nebulae and galaxies stand in the directions Wikidata gives, at the distances of NASA’s pages. The galaxies are shown by Hubble’s photographs, facing the viewer and larger than to scale.

about.Ori: Orion is a hunter of Greek mythology — a giant, a son of Poseidon, the god of the sea. Its seven brightest stars draw an hourglass: four of them make a large rectangle, and in its middle lie the three stars of Orion’s Belt. In one myth Orion boasted that he would kill every animal on Earth, and the angry goddess Gaia sent a scorpion against him (in other tellings it was Artemis or Apollo) — which is given as the reason why Orion and Scorpius are never in the sky at the same time.
about.Tau: Taurus, the Bull, is a constellation of the zodiac, and people have seen a bull in it since very old times. In Greek mythology it is Zeus, who took the form of a magnificent white bull to carry off Europa, a Phoenician princess. Old pictures show only the front half of the bull — explained by his being half under water as he carried Europa out to sea. In another myth it is Io, a lover of Zeus, whom he turned into a heifer to hide her from his wife Hera.
about.Aur: The Latin name Auriga means “the charioteer”. The constellation is drawn as a chariot driver who holds a goat over his left shoulder and two kids under his arm. In Greek mythology he is most often Erichthonius, a king of Athens raised by the goddess Athena: he is credited with inventing the four-horse chariot, and Zeus placed him in the heavens. In another version he is the charioteer Myrtilus, set in the sky after his death by his father Hermes. The brightest star, Capella, is tied to the she-goat Amalthea, who nursed the infant Zeus.
about.Gem: The name is Latin for “twins”: they are Castor and Pollux of Greek mythology, the sons of Leda, both of them Argonauts. In the usual telling they had different fathers: Castor was the mortal son of Tyndareus, king of Sparta, and Pollux the son of Zeus. When Castor died, Pollux begged Zeus to give his brother immortality, and Zeus united them in the heavens. Two bright stars of the constellation bear their names.
about.Per: The constellation is named after Perseus, a hero of Greek mythology and the son of Danaë. King Polydectes sent him to bring the head of Medusa the Gorgon, whose face turned to stone all who looked at her; Perseus slew her in her sleep. Going on, he rescued Andromeda, the daughter of King Cepheus, who was to be sacrificed to a sea monster — in one version he killed it with his sword, in another he turned it to stone with Medusa’s head. In the sky Perseus lies near Andromeda, Cepheus, Cassiopeia, Cetus and Pegasus.
about.Cas: The constellation is named after Cassiopeia of Greek mythology — the queen of Aethiopia, wife of King Cepheus and mother of Andromeda. It is easy to recognise by its “W” of five bright stars. Cassiopeia boasted that her daughter was more beautiful than the Nereids, the sea nymphs (or, in another telling, that she herself was), and the enraged Poseidon sent a sea monster against her country. As a punishment she was placed in the sky on her throne and made to wheel around the north celestial pole, clinging to it half of the time so as not to fall off.
about.And: The constellation is named for Andromeda of the Greek myth, the daughter of Cassiopeia and King Cepheus; in English it is also known as “the Chained Lady”. When Cassiopeia bragged that her daughter was more beautiful than the sea nymphs, Poseidon sent the sea monster Cetus against Aethiopia, and an oracle said that only the sacrifice of the princess would save the kingdom. Andromeda was chained to a rock by the sea, but the hero Perseus saved her — in one version he turned the monster to stone with the head of Medusa, in another he slew it with his sword. They married, and after her death Athena placed Andromeda in the sky. The neighbouring constellations Perseus, Cassiopeia and Cepheus are other characters of the same myth.
about.Peg: The constellation is named after Pegasus, the winged horse of Greek mythology. He was born from the blood of Medusa when Perseus cut off her head. One myth says that his hooves dug out the spring Hippocrene, whose water gave the gift of poetry. Pegasus became the horse of Bellerophon, who killed the Chimera with his help; but when Bellerophon asked to be carried to Mount Olympus, Zeus made the horse throw him off. Three stars of Pegasus and one of Andromeda form the large Square of Pegasus.
about.UMa: Its Latin name means “greater bear”, and many peoples have seen a bear in these stars. Its seven main stars are the Big Dipper, also called the Plough or the Wagon. In the Greek myth the nymph Callisto bore Zeus a son, Arcas, and Zeus’s jealous wife Hera turned her into a bear. When Arcas later met the bear and almost speared her, Zeus whisked them both into the sky: Callisto as Ursa Major and Arcas as Boötes (in another telling, as the Little Bear).
about.UMi: Ursa Minor is Latin for “Lesser Bear”; its seven stars make a smaller ladle, the Little Dipper, with four stars in the bowl. It holds Polaris, the north pole star, and so has long been important to mariners. There is no single myth of it. In one tradition it is a nymph, a nurse of Zeus, whom the god honoured with a place in the sky; in another, two bears saved the infant Zeus from his father Cronus by hiding him on Mount Ida, and he later set them in the sky — their tails growing long as he swung them up.
about.Cyg: Cygnus takes its name from the Latinised Greek word for “swan”; its bright stars form the Northern Cross. In Greek mythology it has been identified with several swans. In one myth it is Zeus, who disguised himself as a swan to seduce Leda, the wife of the Spartan king Tyndareus. In another it is Cygnus, the friend of Phaethon: when Phaethon fell with the Sun’s chariot into the river Eridanus, Cygnus grieved and dived for his bones for many days, and the gods, touched, turned him into a swan and placed him among the stars. Deneb, its brightest star, marks the swan’s tail.
about.Lyr: Lyra is Latin for “lyre”; in Greek mythology it is the lyre of Orpheus, whose music was said to charm even rocks. To reclaim his wife, the nymph Eurydice, Orpheus entered the Underworld, and his playing charmed its god, Hades. Hades let him lead Eurydice back on one condition — never to look back until they were outside. Near the very end Orpheus looked back, and Eurydice was left in the Underworld forever. His lyre was placed in the sky by Zeus.
about.Aql: Its name is Latin for “eagle”. It is often held to be the eagle that carried the thunderbolts of Zeus; the Greek constellation is probably based on a Babylonian Eagle. The same eagle was sent by Zeus to carry Ganymede to Mount Olympus to serve as cup-bearer to the gods (in another telling Zeus himself took the shape of the bird). Other sources say it is the bird that Zeus ordered to attack Prometheus.
about.CMa: Its name is Latin for “greater dog”, in contrast to Canis Minor, the “lesser dog”; both are drawn following Orion, the hunter, through the sky. In Greek mythology Canis Major was the dog Laelaps, a gift from Zeus to Europa — or, in other tellings, a hound so famed for its speed that Zeus raised it to the sky. It was also taken for one of Orion’s hunting dogs, pursuing the Hare. It holds Sirius, the brightest star of the night sky, known as the “dog star”.
about.CMi: Its name is Latin for “lesser dog”; with Canis Major it follows Orion the hunter. The ancient Greeks called it Procyon, “coming before the dog”. One myth links it with Maera, the dog of Icarius of Athens: the dog led Icarius’ daughter Erigone to her father’s body, neither outlived him, and all three were placed in the sky — Erigone as Virgo and Icarius as Boötes. Another connects it with the Teumessian Fox, turned to stone together with its hunter, the dog Laelaps, by Zeus, who placed them in heaven as Canis Minor and Canis Major.
about.Leo: Its name is Latin for “lion”, and its shape recalls a crouching lion. To the ancient Greeks it was the Nemean Lion, whose hide no weapon could pierce. Heracles had to defeat it with his bare hands — the first of his twelve labours — and Zeus commemorated the labour by placing the Lion in the sky.
about.Boo: The name comes from a Greek word for “herdsman” or “ploughman” — literally “ox-driver”: the Greeks saw the nearby Big Dipper as a cart with oxen. Whom Boötes stands for in Greek mythology is not clear. Some myths say that he invented the plough and was set among the stars for it. Another tells of Icarius, taught to make wine by Dionysus: shepherds thought his strong wine had poisoned their friends and killed him, and Zeus honoured him and his daughter Erigone by placing them in the sky as Boötes and Virgo. Arcturus, the name of its brightest star, means “guardian of the bear”.
about.Vir: The name means “maiden” in Latin. The Greeks and Romans identified the constellation with the goddesses Demeter and Persephone, and with Astraea, a goddess of justice, who left the earth and fled to the sky, becoming the constellation. Its star Spica is Latin for “ear of grain”: in Babylon a part of the constellation was “The Furrow” of the goddess Shala with her ear of grain, and so it became associated with fertility. Erigone, the daughter of Icarius, was also seen in it; in the Middle Ages Virgo was associated with the Virgin Mary.
about.Sco: Scorpius is a constellation of the zodiac; the Babylonians already called it the Scorpion. In Greek mythology its story belongs to Orion. In one version Orion boasted to the goddess Artemis and her mother Leto that he would kill every animal on Earth, and they sent a giant scorpion to kill him; in others the scorpion was sent by Apollo or by Gaia. Zeus raised both to the sky, where Orion hunts every winter but flees every summer when the scorpion comes.
about.Oph: The name comes from the Ancient Greek for “serpent-bearer”, and the constellation is drawn as a man grasping a snake — the snake itself is the constellation Serpens. To the ancient Greeks it was the god Apollo struggling with a huge snake that guarded the Oracle of Delphi. Later it was identified with the healer Asclepius, who learned the secret of keeping death at bay by watching one serpent bring another healing herbs; to keep the human race from becoming immortal Jupiter killed him with a bolt of lightning, but later placed his image in the heavens. Another myth names Laocoön, the Trojan priest slain by two sea serpents.

about.m1: What is left of a star that blew up: in 1054 Chinese astronomers saw the explosion in the daytime sky for nearly a month. Today it is a cloud six light-years wide, with a rapidly spinning neutron star — the ultra-dense core of the dead star — at its center. The nebula was discovered by the English astronomer John Bevis in 1731.
about.m2: A ball of over 150,000 stars held together by their own gravity. It is more than 150 light-years across — one of the largest clusters of its kind. Jean-Dominique Maraldi discovered it in 1746 while observing a comet.
about.m3: One of the largest and brightest globular clusters: over 500,000 stars, eight billion years old. It holds more variable stars than any other known cluster. It was the first object of the catalog that Charles Messier discovered himself, in 1764.
about.m4: The globular cluster closest to Earth — a huge ball of stars. It is predicted to hold up to 40,000 white dwarfs: the cores of ancient stars whose outer layers have drifted away. It is relatively easy to find beside the orange-red star Antares. Jean-Philippe Loys de Chéseaux discovered it in 1746.
about.m5: One of the oldest globular clusters of the Milky Way: most of its stars formed more than 12 billion years ago. In binoculars it looks like a patch of light. The German astronomer Gottfried Kirch discovered it in 1702.
about.m7: An open cluster of about 80 stars that formed some 220 million years ago. Claudius Ptolemy recorded it as early as 130 AD — hence its nickname, Ptolemy’s Cluster. It stands right next to the stinger of the Scorpion and is seen best from southern latitudes.
about.m8: A vast cloud of gas and dust where stars are born. The massive young stars inside flood the gas with ultraviolet light and make it shine. The nebula has a star cluster of its own. The Italian astronomer Giovanni Battista Hodierna discovered it in 1654.
about.m10: A bright globular cluster. It is known for its many stars that look far younger than their neighbors. Charles Messier discovered it in 1764.
about.m11: One of the most densely populated open clusters; it formed roughly 220 million years ago. It is named for the V-shaped wedge of its brightest stars. Of the 26 open clusters in Messier’s catalog it is the most distant that can be seen with the naked eye. Gottfried Kirch discovered it in 1681.
about.m13: One of the brightest star clusters of the northern sky: over 100,000 stars. Near its core the stars stand about a hundred times closer together than around our Sun — so close that they sometimes collide. Edmond Halley discovered it in 1714.
about.m15: One of the oldest and densest globular clusters: about 12 billion years old. It was the first globular cluster found to hold a planetary nebula — the gaseous shell of a dying star. Jean-Dominique Maraldi discovered it in 1746.
about.m16: A nebula where stars are born, together with a star cluster. Here stand the famous Pillars of Creation — columns of gas and dust 4 to 5 light-years tall that hide newborn stars; the whole nebula spans 70 by 55 light-years. A small telescope shows the cluster, the pillars need a large one. Jean-Philippe Loys de Chéseaux discovered it in 1745.
about.m17: One of the largest star-forming regions of the Milky Way; it is also called the Swan Nebula. It holds one of our galaxy’s youngest star clusters, only a million years old. The radiation of the young stars evaporates and erodes the cold clouds of gas in which stars form. Jean-Philippe Loys de Chéseaux discovered it in 1745.
about.m20: A nebula where stars are born. It is named for its three bands of thick dust. The young stars flood the gas around them with ultraviolet light and so reshape the nebula itself. Charles Messier discovered it in 1764.
about.m22: One of the globular clusters closest to Earth: a ball of densely packed ancient stars about 70 light-years across. In the sky it takes up as much room as the full Moon. The German amateur Abraham Ihle discovered it in 1665 while looking for Saturn — it is one of the first globular clusters ever found.
about.m24: Not a single object but a clear window between clouds of dust, 600 light-years wide: through it a host of stars of the Sagittarius spiral arm of our galaxy is seen. To the eye it is a hazy patch; binoculars begin to resolve its stars. Charles Messier entered it in his catalog in 1764.
about.m27: The first planetary nebula ever discovered: the shell an old star shed at the end of its life. Such nebulae have nothing to do with planets — the name comes from their round, planet-like look in small telescopes. Charles Messier spotted it in 1764.
about.m31: The nearest major galaxy to our Milky Way. We see it almost edge-on. Hubble has resolved about 200 million stars in it that are hotter than our Sun — only a fraction of all its stars. The first known report of it is in the Book of Fixed Stars by the Persian astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi, from the year 964.
about.m33: The third-largest galaxy of our Local Group after the Andromeda Galaxy and the Milky Way, about half the size of ours. Stars form in it ten times faster than on average in Andromeda. It is one of the most distant objects a keen eye can see unaided — under an exceptionally clear and dark sky.
about.m35: A relatively young open cluster, about 150 million years old. Its approximately 400 stars are spread over some 30 light-years — hot blue stars beside older orange and red giants. The Swiss astronomer Philippe Loys de Chéseaux discovered it in 1745.
about.m42: The closest large star-forming region to Earth: an enormous cloud of dust and gas where vast numbers of new stars are being made. Four massive young stars in its bright middle shape the nebula. The naked eye can spot it just below Orion’s belt; many cultures have known it throughout history.
about.m44: An open cluster of around 1,000 stars, one of the closest to Earth; it is 600 to 700 million years old. It is also known as Praesepe. To the eye it is a blur of light in Cancer, and binoculars show about 20 stars. Galileo was the first to make out stars in it — around forty.
about.m45: An open cluster also called the Seven Sisters: over a thousand stars loosely bound by gravity, of which the eye sees only a handful of the brightest. It has been known since ancient times, so it has no discoverer; Galileo Galilei was the first to look at it through a telescope.
about.m48: An open cluster of middle age: from 100–200 stars at its core to as many as 1,000 in all. Charles Messier recorded it in 1771 at the wrong position, and the cluster was “lost” — it was found again by Johann Elert Bode around 1782 and by Caroline Herschel in 1783.
about.m51: A spiral galaxy. Its arms are star factories: they compress hydrogen gas and make clusters of new stars. Some astronomers think the arms are so prominent because of a close encounter with the small, yellowish galaxy at the tip of one of them. Charles Messier discovered it in 1773.
about.m55: A globular cluster of 100,000 stars about 100 light-years across. It is large and reasonably bright, but it has no dense core and many of its stars are faint — so in binoculars it is only a round hazy patch. It was first spotted in 1752 from what is now South Africa.
about.m57: The glowing remains of a Sun-like star. The blue gas in the middle is in fact an elongated cloud seen end-on, piercing the red doughnut around it. The colors show what it is made of: deep blue is helium, light blue is hydrogen and oxygen, reddish is nitrogen and sulfur. The French astronomer Antoine Darquier de Pellepoix discovered it in 1779.
about.m62: One of the most irregularly shaped globular clusters of our galaxy, almost 12 billion years old. Its very dense core holds 150,000 stars. It is easily found from the bright star Antares. Charles Messier discovered it in 1771.
about.m67: Over 500 stars loosely bound by gravity. Open clusters are usually young, but this is one of the oldest known: about 4 billion years, nearly the age of our Sun. About a hundred of its stars are like the Sun in composition and age. The German astronomer Johann Gottfried Koehler first recorded it in 1779.
about.m71: A ball of ancient stars about 27 light-years across; they are 9 to 10 billion years old. Only in the 1970s did astronomers come to the view that it is a globular cluster, though a rather sparse one. The Swiss astronomer Jean-Philippe de Chéseaux spotted it in the middle of the eighteenth century.
about.m81: One of the brightest galaxies of the night sky. Its spiral arms, which wind all the way down into the nucleus, are made of young, hot, bluish stars. At its center sits a black hole of 70 million solar masses — about 15 times the mass of the Milky Way’s central black hole. The German astronomer Johann Elert Bode discovered it in 1774.
about.m92: One of the brightest and oldest globular clusters of the Milky Way: almost as old as the Universe. About 330,000 stars are tightly packed in it. It orbits the core of our galaxy like a satellite. Johann Elert Bode discovered it in 1777.
about.m104: A spiral galaxy seen nearly edge-on, like a broad-brimmed Mexican hat. Its brilliant white core is encircled by thick lanes of dust. Nearly 2,000 globular clusters surround it — ten times more than the Milky Way has. The French astronomer Pierre Méchain discovered it in 1781.

instruments.title: Instruments of astronomers
instruments.lead: From a rod that casts a shadow to telescopes in space: what people measured the sky with, and how these instruments work.
instruments.drawn: The drawing is made for the program; it is not to scale.
instruments.licence: The text may be used on the same terms:

picture.link: The file’s page on Wikimedia Commons

captions.armillary: An armillary sphere: an engraving from the Encyclopaedia Britannica, 1771.
captions.astrolabe: A page from Johannes Stöffler’s book on the astrolabe, 1524: the instrument is aimed at the top of a tower to measure its height.
captions.quadrant: Tycho Brahe’s mural quadrant at Uraniborg: an engraving from his book of 1598. The observer on the right views a star through the opening at the upper left; one assistant reads the time off a clock, another records the measurements.

gnomon.name: Gnomon and sundial
gnomon.how: A gnomon is an upright rod on level ground, one of the oldest and simplest instruments of astronomy. The length and the direction of its shadow tell how high the Sun stands — and so the time of day. A sundial is the same gnomon with a marked plate: through the day the shadow passes from one hour-line to the next.
gnomon.story: The oldest gnomon known in China is a painted stick of about 2300 BC. The earliest sundials known are Egyptian and Babylonian shadow clocks of about 1500 BC. The philosopher Anaximander is credited with bringing this Babylonian instrument to the Greeks.
gnomon.gave: The time of day — and, from the shadow measured at the solstices, the tilt of the ecliptic to the celestial equator.
gnomon.alt: A drawing: a ray of the Sun passes over the top of an upright rod, whose shadow lies on the ground; the angle between the ground and the ray is the height of the Sun.

armillary.name: Armillary sphere
armillary.how: A model of the sky made of rings. Graduated metal circles stand for the celestial equator, the ecliptic — the apparent path of the Sun on the celestial sphere — meridians and parallels. A small ball usually sits in the middle: the Earth, and in later ones the Sun. It was used to find the coordinates of the lights of the sky.
armillary.story: It was invented separately in China — possibly as early as the 4th century BC — and in Greece in the 3rd century BC. The Greek astronomer Hipparchus credited Eratosthenes as its inventor. Later it was used in the Islamic world and in medieval Europe.
armillary.gave: Before the telescope came in the 17th century, it was the astronomers’ prime instrument for finding positions in the sky.
armillary.alt: A drawing: round a small ball of the Earth stand the circle of a meridian and two rings tilted to each other, the equator and the ecliptic; an axis passes through the poles.

astrolabe.name: Astrolabe
astrolabe.how: A metal disc for both measuring and reckoning. In the hollow of its body, which has a graduated rim, lie flat plates, and over them turns a cut-out frame — the rete — with the circle of the ecliptic and pointers to the brightest stars. It also has a sighting rule: with the astrolabe held upright, one aims the rule at a star or the Sun and reads the height in degrees on the rim.
astrolabe.story: It is essentially a flat version of the armillary sphere. It appeared in Hellenistic times; the sources differ on who invented it, and Hipparchus is often named. Its name is made of the Greek words for “star” and “to take”: it “takes” the height of a star.
astrolabe.gave: The height of a body over the horizon, day or night; it served to identify stars and planets and, given the time, to find the latitude of a place — and the other way round.
astrolabe.alt: A drawing: a disc with a graduated rim and a cut-out star map over it; the sighting rule is aimed at a star, and the angle — the star’s height — is read on the rim.

quadrant.name: Quadrant and mural quadrant
quadrant.how: A quadrant is an instrument that measures angles up to 90°. A mural quadrant is fixed to a wall that stands exactly along the meridian. The observer moves a sight along the arc until the line from it through the sight at the centre of the arc points at the body — and reads its height on the arc.
quadrant.story: The quadrant was first proposed by Ptolemy as a better kind of astrolabe. One of the largest mural quadrants was made by the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe — the last major astronomer to work without a telescope.
quadrant.gave: Positions of the lights of the sky far more accurate than those of any of Tycho Brahe’s predecessors. His assistant Johannes Kepler used these measurements to work out his three laws of planetary motion.
quadrant.alt: A drawing: a wall along the meridian with an opening, and under it a quarter of a circle with degrees; a star’s ray goes through the sight at the centre to the sliding sight on the arc, and the angle is the star’s height.

refractor.name: Refracting telescope
refractor.how: A telescope whose main part is a lens. A large convex lens stands at the front, then comes a long tube, and at the rear an eyepiece. Lenses bend light, as eyeglasses do: the front one gathers the rays of a star, and the eyepiece hands them to the eye.
refractor.story: The first record of such a tube was left about 1608 by Hans Lippershey, a spectacle maker of Middelburg in the Netherlands: he tried to patent it and did not succeed. In 1609 Galileo Galilei heard of the invention, made a tube of his own — with a convex lens at the front and a concave one at the eye — and was the first to observe the sky with it.
refractor.gave: Craters on the Moon, the four largest moons of Jupiter and the phases of Venus.
refractor.inApp: You can fly to these four moons: “Flight” — Jupiter.
refractor.alt: A drawing: the rays of a star pass through a convex lens at the front of a tube, come together and through the concave lens of the eyepiece reach the eye.

reflector.name: Reflecting telescope
reflector.how: A telescope whose main part is a mirror. In Newton’s telescope the light falls on a curved metal mirror at the bottom of the tube and is reflected back towards a focus. A small flat mirror, set at a slant near the focus, turns the beam aside, out of the tube — where it is looked at through an eyepiece.
reflector.story: The first working reflecting telescope was built by Isaac Newton; the sources name different years, from 1668 to 1672. He had noticed that lenses, like prisms, split white light into colors, so that in a telescope of lenses the stars become colored blots.
reflector.gave: Almost all of the major telescopes of today’s science are reflectors. Hubble and Webb are, too.
reflector.alt: A drawing: rays enter an open tube, are reflected by the curved mirror at its bottom, and a small flat mirror turns them aside, to the eyepiece and the eye.

spectroscope.name: Spectroscope
spectroscope.how: An instrument that spreads light into a spectrum — a band of colors. The light of a star passes through a narrow slit, and then a prism or a diffraction grating spreads it by wavelength. A hot solid body gives a continuous spectrum, a hot gas shines only at particular wavelengths, and when a hot body is surrounded by cooler gas, dark lines appear in the spectrum — where that gas would shine.
spectroscope.story: It began in the 17th century, when Isaac Newton passed a beam of sunlight through a prism. The first modern spectroscope — a prism, a slit and a telescope together — was made by Joseph von Fraunhofer. In the 1850s Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen explained where the dark lines come from.
spectroscope.gave: What the stars are made of: by comparing the dark lines with the lines of known gases, their chemical composition is found. In 1863 William Huggins proved with a spectroscope that the stars consist of the same elements that exist on the Earth.
spectroscope.alt: A drawing: the light of a star passes through a slit and a prism, fans out into colors and falls as a band — the spectrum — in which dark lines are seen.

plate.name: Photographic plate
plate.how: A photographic plate is put into a telescope in place of the eye. Unlike the eye, it gathers light for a long time, so a picture taken with a long exposure shows what the eye cannot see. Large telescopes came to be built as big cameras.
plate.story: The first to try to photograph the Moon was Louis Daguerre, the inventor of the daguerreotype, in 1839. The first successful photograph of the Moon was made on March 23, 1840, by John William Draper: an exposure of 20 minutes, a 13 cm reflecting telescope. The first star other than the Sun — Vega — was photographed in July 1850 at Harvard College Observatory.
plate.gave: Hundreds of thousands of new stars and nebulae invisible to the eye.
plate.alt: A drawing: the faint light of a star passes through the lens of a telescope and gathers on a photographic plate; a clock shows that the light is gathered for a long time.

radio.name: Radio telescope
radio.how: An antenna with a radio receiver that catches radio waves from the sky. It is usually a large dish — a curved metal mirror that may be made of mesh and tens of meters across: it gathers the radio waves at its focus, where the receiver stands.
radio.story: Radio waves from space were first noticed in the early 1930s by the engineer Karl Jansky — with an antenna built to study the noise of radio receivers. He concluded that the hiss came from the Milky Way and was strongest from the direction of the center of the Galaxy, in the constellation of Sagittarius. The first purpose-built radio telescope — a nine-meter dish — was put up in 1937 by the radio amateur Grote Reber in his back yard.
radio.gave: Pulsars and quasars, and radio “pictures” of galaxies, of nebulae and even of the radio emissions of planets.
radio.alt: A drawing: radio waves fall from above on a large dish, are reflected by it and meet at the focus, where the receiver stands.

hubble.name: Hubble Space Telescope
hubble.how: The first astronomical observatory in orbit round the Earth that records images in light from ultraviolet to near infrared. The light falls on the main mirror, is reflected to a smaller, second mirror, and that one sends it back through a hole in the main mirror — to the cameras and spectrographs. Why in space: the Earth’s air blocks some light altogether, and its shifting pockets blur the images — they are also why the stars twinkle.
hubble.story: It was launched on April 24, 1990, aboard the space shuttle Discovery. It flies round the Earth a few hundred kilometers up — above the atmosphere.
hubble.gave: It was the first telescope to detect and analyze the atmosphere of a planet outside the Solar System.
hubble.inApp: Hubble’s photographs are in the cards of the galaxies, nebulae and clusters on the sky map.
hubble.alt: A drawing: the telescope above the Earth’s atmosphere; the light is reflected from the main mirror to the second mirror and goes through a hole in the main one to the cameras.

webb.name: James Webb Space Telescope
webb.how: An infrared telescope. Its main mirror is made of 18 hexagonal segments that act as one large curved mirror; each has a very thin coating of gold, which reflects infrared light better. To detect the faint heat of distant objects, the mirrors and the sensors must be kept extremely cold, so a sunshield protects the telescope from light and heat.
webb.story: It was launched on December 25, 2021, from French Guiana on an Ariane 5 rocket. It orbits the Sun 1.5 million kilometers from the Earth. It was formerly known as the Next Generation Space Telescope; in 2002 it was renamed after a former NASA administrator.
webb.gave: The era when the first stars and galaxies formed; stars shrouded in clouds of dust; water in the atmospheres of other worlds.
webb.alt: A drawing: over the sunshield stands the main mirror of gold segments; the light is reflected from it to the second mirror and back, to the instruments. The Sun is on the other side of the shield.

labels.hot: the Sun is on this side

far.label: Beyond the Solar System
far.scene: A model: the Milky Way, the Sun’s place in it, star clusters, nebulae and the neighbouring galaxies. The list of buttons below says what is where; the arrow keys turn the model, plus and minus change the scale, Enter names what is in the middle.

notes.near: The clusters and nebulae of the sky map, in their places round the Sun. The line from a mark shows how far above or below the plane of the Galaxy it stands. Drag to turn; touch a mark to open its card.
notes.galaxy: The Milky Way from outside is an artist’s concept by NASA: nobody has photographed it from there. The Sun and the clusters are placed by NASA’s distances. Drag to turn; touch a mark to open its card.
notes.group: The galaxies are shown by Hubble’s photographs — as they are seen from the Earth; nobody has seen them from another side. Their sizes are enlarged: at this scale each would be a dot. Touch a galaxy to fly to it.
notes.far: The galaxies are shown by Hubble’s photographs — as they are seen from the Earth; nobody has seen them from another side. Their sizes are enlarged: at this scale each would be a dot. Touch a galaxy to fly to it.
notes.sun: We are here. In NASA’s words, the Earth is in one of the spiral arms, about halfway from the middle of the Galaxy; the Solar System takes about 240 million years to go once round the middle.
notes.arrived: {name}: Hubble’s photograph, enlarged. The light we see in it took {years} to reach us. Touch the photograph or the “i” button to open its card.
notes.nothing: None of the marks is in the middle. Turn the model or change the scale.
